headline: CMF Buds Neo Review | Stylish, affordable earbuds punch above their price
body: The third member of the Neo family, the CMF Buds Neo, looks to bring a well-tested combination of style, useful features and good audio at an even more accessible price than its predecessor
full_body:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

The third member of the Neo family, the CMF Buds Neo , looks to bring a well-tested combination of style, useful features and good audio at an even more accessible price than its predecessor. At ₹1,999, the Buds Neo comes with features such as ANC, dual connectivity and a Nothing X app, making them an interesting option in the budget TWS segment.

The CMF Buds Neo continues the brand’s familiar design language with a square charging case, rounded corners and a matte finish. The rotating ring in the corner now doubles as a lanyard attachment, while the USB Type-C port and LED indicator keep things simple.

The earbuds themselves combine matte stems with a glossy main body and feel quite well-built for the price. They are also extremely light, and I found them comfortable even during longer listening sessions. The included silicone tips in three sizes make it easier to find a secure fit, while the IP54 rating adds some protection against dust, sweat and light splashes. You can wear them to gym.

The Buds Neo uses 12.4mm dynamic drivers and goes for a warm, bass-forward sound signature. The bass gets plenty of emphasis, while the mids remain reasonably clear and the treble takes a slight back seat.

I enjoyed this tuning for casual listening, particularly with bass-heavy Bollywood tracks and game soundtracks. Softer tracks also sounded pleasant, although these earbuds are clearly not aimed at listeners looking for a neutral presentation. The Nothing X app offers six EQ presets, giving you some control over the sound.

The biggest surprise here is the ANC. The Buds Neo offers up to 35dB of noise cancellation, and it works quite well for the price. It does a fine job of reducing constant background sounds in offices, cafeterias and at home, while traffic noise is softened even if it isn’t completely eliminated.

full_body:

Google has rolled out a new AI feature known as Expert Intelligence that allows readers to use AI in order to get personalised insights from the e-books they bought through Google Play Books.

To make use of the feature, readers can upload eligible e-books into a Gemini Notebook. Following this, they can use AI to ask questions, understand the book, generate infographics, create audio overviews, generate quizzes, or even make action plans by uploading their own notes and ideas.

Google cited the hypothetical example of a manager brainstorming strategies in line with a management book, a woman uploading journal entries in order to benefit from the information provided in an e-book about menopause, or a family creating a meal plan inspired by a food culture book.

Expert Intelligence would allow them to apply lessons from their respective books to their own lives.

However, company-based restrictions mean that readers must buy the books they want to analyse with AI from Google Play Books. While the AI Notebook can be shared with others, they too must buy the book in order to engage with the content fully.

More readers are using AI in order to summarise or analyse the books they are reading , but these features rarely exist on one platform. Readers may need to “jailbreak” copyright protections to allow external AI tools to view their e-books. Others opt to run pirated copies through AI systems for ease. A clunkier method involves copying and pasting sections of books into AI chatbots to ask for highly specific and personalised assistance.

headline: Is memory chip crunch wiping out ₹10K smartphone market in India?
body: As per an IDC estimate, nearly 173 million sub-₹10K smartphones, which shipped last year, are facing an existential crisis. In Q2 2026, this segment saw an almost 60% YoY drop
full_body:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

As memory chip crunch is forcing brands to repeated price hikes across smartphone segments , the budget tier seems to be facing an existential crisis as the margin in this segment has always been the thinnest. As per an IDC estimate, nearly 173 million sub-₹10K smartphones, which shipped last year, are facing an existential crisis. In Q2 2026, this segment [below $100 smartphone] saw an almost 60% year-over-year (YoY) drop. The decline is expected to continue for the rest of this year.

Memory prices are soaring with over 300% YoY increase, per IDC, and the trend is expected to continue until 2028. Smartphone makers will eventually move to a mid and premium segments to minimise the cost burden and help the market grow in value over volume.

“To make a ₹10,000 phone now, you have to first buy a memory worth ₹4,000 to ₹4,500 and then think of adjusting BoM (bill of material) like display, SoC, camera, battery and then also make some room for margins which look extremely difficult. Hence, it won’t be wrong to say that sub-₹10k category staring at a complete wipeout unless someone sells them at loss or change business model,” says Tarun Pathak, Research Director at Counterpoint. He added that this segment will under immense pressure for the next 18 months. “Some older phones may still be sold or even second-hand phones will find [a place] in sub-₹10,000 [segment].”

The segment’s share has dropped from 19% in Q2 2025 to just 4% in Q2 2026, and sales has declined 81% YoY. Even the ₹10,000–₹20,000 segment has declined 7%, as some devices are now moving above ₹20,000 following price hikes. This is gradually reshaping the affordable smartphone market, with consumers having to compromise on specifications or stretch their budgets to access better devices.

“The sub-₹10,000 segment isn’t just under pressure; it’s disappearing in real time,” Upasana Joshi, Senior Research Manager at IDC India/SEA said. “Brands have responded [to the memory chip price rise] by cutting model launches and pulling back-channel support rather than eating the increase themselves.”

Smartphone makers are relaunching 4G phones at a time when customers are looking to upgrade smartphones that can provide them better cellular connectivity and generative AI features.

headline: DPDP Act: are compliance costs of privacy law crushing ed-tech businesses?
body: For an industry built on collecting exactly the kind of data the law now regulates — names, quiz scores, attendance records, AI tutoring conversations, sometimes biometric identifiers — the compliance bill is proving to be substantial
full_body:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

When Mihir Jana’s IT team sits down with a new client these days, the conversation no longer starts only with features or pricing. Instead, they ask more about where the data is going and how long it will be kept.

Mr. Jana is the managing director of EDZLearn Services, a Delhi-based company that builds learning management systems and AI-driven platforms for schools, universities, banks, and other institutions. Since India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act began taking effect, he said, “the entire ballgame has changed” for the ed-tech industry his company serves.

Passed by the Parliament in August 2023 and rolled out in phases since the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, the law is reshaping how education technology companies collect, store and delete the personal data of schoolchildren, some of India’s youngest and most vulnerable internet users.

The Data Protection Board of India became operational the same month the rules were notified; penalties and a consent manager registration system are due to take effect in November, and full compliance covering consent, breach reporting, audits and data principal rights becomes mandatory by May, 2027.

For an industry built on collecting exactly the kind of data the law now regulates — names, quiz scores, attendance records, AI tutoring conversations, sometimes biometric identifiers — the compliance bill is proving to be substantial. The price tag can be huge and vary sharply depending on the size of the business, the sector it operates in, and the amount of risk it is prepared to carry. This has become one of the more contentious corners of the DPDP rollout.

Though Mr. Jana declined to put a hard number on the cost, he confirmed that figures circulating in the industry, roughly ₹3 lakh to ₹8 lakh a month for a general-purpose platform, are “a good figure.” The costs rise sharply in regulated sectors. “For a bank to adhere to the DPDP Act, the cost will go up to ₹12-15 lakh,” he said, and healthcare clients handling medical data push costs higher still.

headline: India tribunal lifts WhatsApp data-sharing ban, upholds Meta fine
body: WhatsApp had challenged the Competition Commission of India's November 2024 ban on data sharing between WhatsApp and other Meta entities, warning it may have to roll back some features
full_body:

An Indian appeals tribunal on Tuesday set aside an antitrust watchdog's five-year ban on Meta-owned WhatsApp sharing user data with other Meta entities for advertising, but upheld a fine, marking a partial win for the U.S. tech major.

WhatsApp had challenged the Competition Commission of India's November 2024 ban on data sharing between WhatsApp and other Meta entities, warning it may have to roll back some features.

Meta also criticised the CCI for not having the "technical expertise" to understand the ramifications of its order.

The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) lifted the data-sharing ban, noting that "the rationale for the...ban was missing altogether".

However, it upheld the $25.4 million fine that the CCI had imposed, saying Meta abused its dominance by imposing unfair conditions.

India is Meta's biggest market with the highest number of users on Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp worldwide.

headline: Stock market today: Sensex, Nifty eye higher opening as crude oil prices fall
body: Indian stock markets will remain in focus on Wednesday as investors assess whether falling crude oil prices can provide further support to equities a
full_body:
The Indian rupee ended Tuesday at 95.4125 per dollar, marking its best session in about a month as easing oil prices provided support. Sustained intervention by the central bank also helped curb further weakness in the currency.

The rupee's recovery came alongside a sharp decline in crude oil prices, with Brent falling 3% to $89.32 a barrel during Tuesday's session. Currency trading will remain closed on Wednesday for a local holiday and will resume on Thursday.

Global investors are bracing for Nvidia's quarterly earnings on Wednesday, with the results expected to provide fresh clues about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence spending boom.

Asian markets were mixed ahead of the results, while investors are watching whether Nvidia's performance and outlook can support the broader technology trade.

The focus comes as global markets continue to assess bond yields, oil prices and expectations around inflation. Nvidia's earnings could therefore influence sentiment across global technology and semiconductor stocks as Indian markets begin Wednesday's session.

Foreign portfolio investors remained net buyers of Indian equities for the second consecutive session on Tuesday, providing support to domestic markets. FPIs bought shares worth Rs 1,594 crore on Tuesday, according to provisional NSE data.

Domestic institutional investors also remained buyers, recording inflows of Rs 230 crore.

The buying came as Indian benchmark indices ended higher, with the Sensex gaining 286.98 points and the Nifty rising 115.50 points. Investors will continue to track domestic institutional flows and global cues as the market heads into Wednesday's session.
